messages.content:
RoadDraft is a headless 2D CAD engine for roadway plans. Model space is US survey feet, and a point is [x, y] = [easting, northing] -- the other way round from how coordinates are usually spoken, so N 7300, E 4100 is [4100, 7300]. Sheets are paper inches seen through viewports at a feet-per-inch scale. Work through the commands: each one validates its params and explains what was wrong, every change is journaled and undoable. Start with get_document_state to see what is in the document, list_commands for the full surface, and render_sheet or render_model to look at your work.

To annotate something, find it before you point at it. In a sheet file the design usually lives in a referenced basefile, so the document owns no geometry of its own; find_entities searches the attachments too. Filter by what a thing IS -- layer, type, or its design anchor -- rather than dumping the document: find_entities {anchor: {kind: 'offset', offset: [-15, 15]}, visible_on: 'P-202'} is the pavement edges that sheet shows. Then pass the id straight to place_callout as target_entity, and the engine puts the leader tip on the geometry. Do not compute the point yourself: the midpoint of a curve's endpoints is not on the curve, and roadway linework runs parallel a few feet apart, so a hand-computed point usually lands on the wrong line rather than on nothing. If you do pass a raw target point, read the warning that comes back -- it names what the tip actually touched.

Some things are not entities at all -- a station, a PC, a point at an offset. Ask the design for those: list_alignments with include_references=true names a referenced alignment 'BASE:RTE-7', and station_to_xy, xy_to_station, resolve_anchor and get_design_data all accept that name and answer in host coordinates. To call one out, give place_callout a target_anchor ('86+50@15R', 'PC-2'; BC-2 and EC-2 name the PC and PT too) and that alignment name. Otherwise commands do not take it: nothing can be drawn, labelled or anchored to an alignment this document does not own.

Plan annotation belongs on the sheet, in paper inches, not in the model. Pass the sheet as place_callout's space and still name a model target -- target_entity or target_anchor: the engine sees it through the sheet's viewport (scale and twist included) and puts the tip where it shows on the paper. 'at' then runs along the part of the entity that sheet shows, since a pavement edge runs the whole project and a sheet shows one stretch. find_entities with visible_on gives each row a sheet_point, which is where that tip will land -- use it to choose a position for the text that is clear of the linework. Never work out a viewport by hand: model_to_sheet and sheet_to_model convert, and station_to_xy and point_on_entity take a sheet and answer in paper inches as well.

Drafting from a description works the same way: give the engine the description, not coordinates you worked out. A bearing and distance goes in as written -- create_alignment takes start + legs (each leg a bearing, azimuth or deflection and the distance to the next PI, with the radius of the curve at the PI it starts from), draw_traverse draws lines and curves course by course, and traverse computes the points without drawing. offset_entity copies linework parallel at a distance (one entity, or a chain offset as one path), fillet rounds the corner between two lines with a curve (a curb return), and measure with along gives distances along a line, chain or alignment and square off it. key_points and snap give the exact endpoints, intersections, centers and alignment design points (PI, BC, EC) to build on. Station-and-offset drafting is draw_station_offset with the stations and offsets given ('82+00@15R'). Linework drawn through something is cut back with trim (a point on the part to cut away) or run on with extend, not redrawn from computed points; break, join, lengthen, chamfer, copy, rotate, mirror, scale and array edit what is there. create_points sets COGO points, label_segments letters bearings and distances or L1/C1 tags with line and curve tables, place_along sets blocks or points at an interval, hatch fills an area (a point inside is enough), and area and get_entity read areas, lengths, bearings and curve data off the drawing.

Do one drafting task in a headless CAD engine called RoadDraft, using the tools you have been given. They are your ENTIRE tool surface.

Rules:
- Every change to the drawing must go through a tool call.
- The document is already open and saves itself after each command. Do not save it under another name.
- Nobody can answer questions. Work until you judge the task done, then stop and give your report.
- You have no calculator and no code execution. Any arithmetic you need, do yourself.

THE TASK:
Draft the design model for ELM-AVE. The alignment begins at N 3000.00, E 1000.00, station 10+00. It runs S 80°00'00" E for 800.00 ft to PI-1, where it deflects 40°00'00" to the left on a 500 ft radius curve; then 700.00 ft to PI-2, where it deflects 25°00'00" to the right on a 700 ft radius curve; then 600.00 ft to its end. It has two 11 ft lanes and 5 ft shoulders. Draw the centerline on align_MAIN, the edges of pavement on rd_EP and the outside edges of shoulder on rd_ES, and label the stations every 100 ft.

When finished, reply briefly with:
1. What you created and drew (names, layers, key coordinates).
2. The tool calls that mattered, in order (tool name + the key arguments).
3. Anything that failed, confused you, or that you had to work around -- quote error messages. If you had to compute coordinates yourself, show the arithmetic.

First, let me understand the task:

1. Create the alignment ELM-AVE:
   - Starting point N 3000.00, E 1000.00 → model coordinates [1000, 3000] (x=easting, y=northing)
   - Station 10+00 (begin_station)
   - S 80°00'00" E, 800.00 ft to PI-1
   - At PI-1: deflect 40°00'00" left, curve radius 500 ft
   - Next 700.00 ft to PI-2
   - At PI-2: deflect 25°00'00" right, curve radius 700 ft
   - Next 600.00 ft to the end point

2. Two 11 ft lanes = 22 ft total pavement width → pavement edge is offset ±11 ft from centerline
   - 5 ft shoulders on each side → shoulder outside edge is offset ±16 ft

3. Draw:
   - Centerline on align_MAIN
   - Pavement edges (±11) on rd_EP
   - Shoulder outside edges (±16) on rd_ES
   - Station labels every 100 ft

create_alignment tool takes start + legs. Legs are:
- leg 1: bearing "S 80°00'00\" E", distance 800 (from start to PI-1). The radius is the curve at the PI where this leg begins — this leg starts at BEGIN, no curve there, so no radius.
- leg 2: from PI-1 to PI-2: deflection 40° left at PI-1, radius 500, distance 700.
- leg 3: from PI-2 to end: deflection 25° right at PI-2, radius 700, distance 600.

Wait, let me re-read the leg semantics: "legs: the layout as bearings and distances, PI to PI from start… radius is the curve at the PI where this leg starts (legs after the first)."

So:
- leg 1: {bearing: "S 80°00'00\" E", distance: 800} — from BEGIN to PI-1.
- leg 2: {deflection: "40 L", radius: 500, distance: 700} — from PI-1 to PI-2, with the 40° left deflection at PI-1 and radius 500.
- leg 3: {deflection: "25 R", radius: 700, distance: 600} — from PI-2 to END, with the 25° right deflection at PI-2 and radius 700.

begin_station: "10+00" (1000 ft).

Next, drawing:
- draw_alignment on layer align_MAIN.
- draw_offset with alignment, offsets [-11, 11] on rd_EP.
- draw_offset with offsets [-16, 16] on rd_ES.

Plan for tool calls:

2. create_layer align_MAIN, create_layer rd_EP, create_layer rd_ES. (independent — can be batched)

Let me think through the geometry to double-check results later (no calculator, but I can do the math by hand):

Start: [1000, 3000].

Bearing S 80° E: azimuth = 180° - 80° = 100°. Direction: dx = sin(az), dy = cos(az). Azimuth 100°: dx = sin(100°) = 0.984807753, dy = cos(100°) = -0.173648178.

800 ft to PI-1: dx = 800 × 0.984807753 = 787.846202, dy = 800 × (-0.173648178) = -138.918542.
PI-1 = [1787.846202, 2861.081458].

At PI-1, 40° left deflection. In a survey traverse, left deflection = counterclockwise? In standard survey practice, right deflections are clockwise (increase of azimuth), left deflections are counterclockwise (decrease of azimuth).

Azimuth of leg 1 = 100°. Left deflection 40° → new azimuth = 100° - 40° = 60°.

Leg 2, 700 ft, azimuth 60°: dx = 700 × sin(60°) = 700 × 0.866025404 = 606.217782, dy = 700 × cos(60°) = 700 × 0.5 = 350.
PI-2 = [1787.846202 + 606.217782, 2861.081458 + 350] = [2394.063984, 3211.081458].

At PI-2, 25° right deflection: new azimuth = 60° + 25° = 85°.
Leg 3, 600 ft, azimuth 85°: dx = 600 × sin(85°) = 600 × 0.996194698 = 597.716819, dy = 600 × cos(85°) = 600 × 0.087155743 = 52.293446.
END = [2394.063984 + 597.716819, 3211.081458 + 52.293446] = [2991.780803, 3263.374904].

Stations:
- BEGIN: 10+00 (1000)
- Tangent 1: 800 ft → PI-1 tangent is at 1080.
- Curve 1: Δ=40°, R=500. L = R × Δ(rad) = 500 × (40 × π/180) = 500 × 0.698131701 = 349.065850 ft. T = R × tan(Δ/2) = 500 × tan(20°) = 500 × 0.363970234 = 181.985117 ft.
  PC-1 = 1080 - 181.985117 = 898.014883 → 08+98.01 (raw station).
  PT-1 = PC-1 + 349.065850 = 1247.080733 → 12+47.08.
  Tangent 2 begins at 1247.08.
- Tangent 2: from PT-1 to PI-2. Distance from PI-1 to PI-2 is 700 (tangent distance, i.e. the straight-line distance between the PIs? No, wait!).

Hmm, actually I need to think about what "distance to the next PI" means in a PI-based layout. In classic circular curve layout, the legs of the traverse are the tangent distances from one PI to the next — the straight lines connecting the PIs. The alignment itself is a tangent from BEGIN to PC-1, an arc, a tangent to PT-2, an arc, and a tangent to END. The stationing is along the alignment (tangent + arc + tangent + arc + tangent), not along the PI traverse.

So in create_alignment's legs, each leg's distance is the PI-to-PI tangent distance, and the radius belongs to the curve at the PI where the leg begins. The engine computes the actual alignment geometry and stations.

So:
- Tangent 1 (BEGIN to PC-1): 800 - 181.985117 = 618.014883 ft.
- Curve 1: L = 349.065850.
- Tangent 2 (PT-1 to PT-2): PI-1 to PI-2 is 700; tangent 2 = 700 - T1 - T2, where T2 = R2 tan(Δ2/2) = 700 × tan(12.5°) = 700 × 0.221694664 = 155.186265 ft. So tangent 2 = 700 - 181.985117 - 155.186265 = 362.828618 ft.
- Curve 2: Δ=25°, R=700. L = 700 × (25 × π/180) = 700 × 0.436332313 = 305.432619 ft.
- Tangent 3 (PT-2 to END): 600 - 155.186265 = 444.813735 ft.

Total length = 618.014883 + 349.065850 + 362.828618 + 305.432619 + 444.813735 = let me add:
618.014883 + 349.065850 = 967.080733
967.080733 + 362.828618 = 1329.909351
1329.909351 + 305.432619 = 1635.341970
1635.341970 + 444.813735 = 2080.155705 ft.

END station = 1000 + 2080.155705 = 3080.155705 → 30+80.16.

Stations:

- PT-1: 1000 + 967.080733 = 1967.080733 → 19+67.08

Station ticks every 100 ft from 10+00: 10+00, 11+00, 12+00, ..., 30+00 (the last 100 tick at 30+00 is before END 30+80.16).

messages.reasoning:
The document is new, and the required layers (align_MAIN, rd_EP, rd_ES) already exist. So let's create the alignment.

Layout description:
- Start point: N 3000.00, E 1000.00 → [1000, 3000], station 10+00
- Leg 1: S 80°00'00" E, distance 800.00, to PI-1
- PI-1: left deflection 40°, R=500, then a 700.00 ft tangent to PI-2
- PI-2: right deflection 25°, R=700, then 600.00 ft to endpoint

In create_alignment, legs are described as "the tangent from one PI to the next: direction and distance to the next PI; radius is the curve at the PI where this leg begins." Hmm, let me read carefully:

"legs: the layout as bearing and distance, PI to PI from start -- as described in the report: 'S 76° E 650 ft to PI-2, where left deflection 33° onto a 450 ft curve; then 820 ft...' is [{bearing: 'S 76 E', distance: 650}, {deflection: '33 L', radius: 450, distance: 820}, ...]"

So the format is: each leg describes the tangent from the current PI to the next PI. The deflection/radius attached to a leg is the curve at the PI where that leg "begins" (i.e., the previous PI). Wait, let me reread.

From the schema: "legs: one tangent from PI to next: direction (exactly one of bearing, azimuth, deflection, angle_right) and distance to next PI; radius is the curve at the PI where this leg begins (legs after the first)."

So for a leg:
- Direction of the tangent (first leg is from the start; subsequent legs... hmm, but "deflection" is listed as a direction option). Actually, in the draw_traverse tool, deflection is "the angle turned from the previous course" — i.e., it describes the direction of this leg relative to the previous leg.

So the legs here:
- Leg 1: bearing S 80°00'00" E, distance 800.00 (tangent from BEGIN to PI-1). No deflection (first leg).
- Leg 2: deflection 40 L (the angle turned at PI-1 from leg 1), radius 500 (curve at PI-1 where leg 2 begins), distance 700.00 (tangent from PI-1 to PI-2).
- Leg 3: deflection 25 R (angle turned at PI-2), radius 700 (curve at PI-2 where leg 3 begins), distance 600.00 (tangent from PI-2 to END).
